_meta.descricao: The four parts of the Catechism of the Catholic Church and what each one sets forth.
_meta.aviso: Presents the structure of the four parts of the Catechism of the Catholic Church — it is not a summary of its content and does not replace reading it directly.

itens.titulo: Part One: The Profession of Faith
itens.resumo: The part of the Catechism devoted to what the Church believes: from the search for God and Revelation to the response of faith, and the exposition of the Apostles' Creed and the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed, article by article.
itens.corpo:
Part One of the Catechism of the Catholic Church is entitled "The Profession of Faith" and spans paragraphs 26 to 1065. It answers the question "in whom and in what do we believe" and, according to the work itself, sets out the faith "professed" — the first of the four dimensions by which the Catechism is organized (faith professed, celebrated, lived, and prayed). It is divided into two Sections. The first, "I Believe" – "We Believe" (nos. 26-184), considers man as "capable" of God, that is, the desire for God written in the human heart, followed by the Revelation with which God comes to meet him and the response of faith, both personal and ecclesial. The second Section, "The Profession of the Christian Faith" (nos. 185-1065), goes through the Creed article by article.

The Catechism first establishes the two Creeds that structure the exposition. The Apostles' Creed is presented as "the ancient baptismal symbol of the Church of Rome", whose authority comes from its being "the Creed that the Roman Church, the See of Peter the first of the apostles, guards" (nos. 194, citing Saint Ambrose, *Explanatio Symboli*). To it is added the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed, which "draws its great authority from the fact that it stems from the first two ecumenical Councils (in 325 and 381)" and "remains common to all the great Churches of both East and West" (no. 195). The exposition follows the Apostles' Creed — "as it were, the oldest Roman catechism" — completed by constant references to the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed, generally more explicit (no. 196).

The second Section is organized into three chapters, distributed according to the three divine Persons: "I Believe in God the Father" (nos. 198-421), on creation and the fall; "I Believe in Jesus Christ, the Only Begotten Son of God" (nos. 422-682), on the Incarnation, the Passion, death, Resurrection, and Ascension; and "I Believe in the Holy Spirit" (nos. 683-1065), which gathers together faith in the Church, the communion of saints, the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the body, and life everlasting.

It is worth placing the work in its historical context. In October 1985, the Extraordinary Assembly of the Synod of Bishops, held twenty years after the close of the Second Vatican Council, asked for the composition of a catechism of all Catholic doctrine. In 1986, John Paul II entrusted the task to a commission of twelve cardinals and bishops chaired by the then Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, assisted by an editorial committee of seven diocesan bishops who were experts in theology and catechesis. The text was promulgated by the Apostolic Constitution *Fidei depositum*, of October 11, 1992 — the thirtieth anniversary of the opening of the Council — and the Latin typical edition, revised and definitive, was approved by the Apostolic Letter *Laetamur magnopere*, of August 15, 1997.

This First Part is, therefore, the doctrinal foundation on which the following three rest: what the faith confesses, says the Catechism, the sacraments communicate (cf. no. 1692), and it is from the Creed that both the liturgy and the moral life and prayer are understood.

itens.titulo: Part One: The Revelation of God
itens.resumo: The article of the Catechism that explains how God, in his goodness and wisdom, chooses to reveal himself and to communicate the mystery of his plan of salvation.
itens.corpo:
Within the chapter "God Comes to Meet Man," this article deals with God's plan to reveal and communicate himself, culminating in Jesus Christ, "the mediator and the fullness of all Revelation." It traces the stages of Revelation throughout the history of salvation: the Covenant with Noah, the call of Abraham, the formation of the people of Israel through Moses and the prophets, up to the Son, who is the definitive and unsurpassable Word of the Father.

The text also explains why this Revelation had to be handed on to all generations and why, even so, it is "complete," with no new public revelation to be expected before the glorious manifestation of Christ. It is the foundation on which the following articles rest, which deal with how this Revelation reaches us.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part One, Section I, Chapter II, Article 1, nos. 50-67
Second Vatican Council, Dogmatic Constitution "Dei Verbum" (1965), nos. 2-4

itens.titulo: Part One: The Transmission of Divine Revelation
itens.resumo: How God's Revelation reaches us: apostolic Tradition, Sacred Scripture, and the living Magisterium of the Church.
itens.corpo:
This article explains that Christ commanded the Apostles to proclaim the Gospel to every creature, and that this transmission takes place in two closely connected ways: apostolic Tradition, alive in the Church, and Sacred Scripture, "the speech of God as it is put down in writing under the breath of the Holy Spirit." The Catechism insists that Scripture and Tradition "make up a single sacred deposit of the Word of God."

It also sets out the role of the Magisterium — the office of authentically interpreting the Word of God, entrusted to the Bishops in communion with the successor of Peter — and the organic relationship among Scripture, Tradition, and the Magisterium, "so linked and joined together that one cannot stand without the others."
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part One, Section I, Chapter II, Article 2, nos. 74-100
Second Vatican Council, Dogmatic Constitution "Dei Verbum" (1965), nos. 7-10

itens.titulo: Part One: Sacred Scripture
itens.resumo: The inspiration and truth of the Bible, the canon of the sacred books, and the Catholic principles for interpreting Scripture.
itens.corpo:
This article deals with the Bible as a book inspired by God, whose authors are the human hagiographers and, at the same time, God as principal author, "teaching firmly, faithfully, and without error that truth which God, for the sake of our salvation, wished to see confided to the Sacred Scriptures." It explains the unity between the Old and the New Testament and presents the canon of the sacred books recognized by the Church.

The Catechism also sets out the criteria for a correct interpretation of Scripture — attention to the content and unity of the whole of Scripture, reading it within the living Tradition of the Church, and respect for the analogy of faith — as well as the literal and spiritual senses (allegorical, moral, and anagogical) that Christian exegesis has traditionally recognized in the sacred text.

It concludes the first section of Part One, which deals with "how we believe," before the second section moves on to the content of the faith professed in the Creed.

itens.titulo: Creed: "I believe in God, the Father almighty, Creator of heaven and earth"
itens.resumo: The Catechism's commentary on the first article of the Creed: the attributes of God, the Most Holy Trinity, creation, man in the image of God, and original sin.
itens.corpo:
Opening its exposition of the Apostles' Creed, this chapter comments on the formula "I believe in God, the Father almighty, Creator of heaven and earth", going through, in subsections, what it means to believe in God, the mystery of God as Father, divine omnipotence, and God as Creator. It is here that the Catechism sets out the Trinitarian faith — one God in three Persons — and the dogma of creation out of nothing, including the invisible world of the angels and the visible world.

The chapter then deals with man, created in the image and likeness of God, male and female, body and soul, established at the beginning in a state of original justice and holiness. Finally, it sets out the doctrine of the fall: the account in Genesis of the first sin and the dogma of original sin, transmitted to all humanity by propagation and not by imitation, which wounds human nature without destroying it — closing with the promise of a Redeemer already announced in Genesis 3:15.

It is one of the longest chapters of the Catechism, since it brings together themes of metaphysics, theological cosmology and Christian anthropology under the first article of the Creed.

itens.titulo: Creed: "Jesus Christ, His only Son, our Lord"
itens.resumo: The Catechism's commentary on the names and titles of Jesus in the Creed: Jesus, Christ, only Son of God, Lord.
itens.corpo:
Opening the chapter dedicated to Jesus Christ, the Catechism comments, one by one, on the names and titles confessed in the Creed. It explains the meaning of the name "Jesus" ("God saves"), of the title "Christ" (the Anointed One, the Messiah awaited by Israel), of the expression "only Son of God" — which affirms the eternal and unique sonship of Christ, distinct from the adoptive sonship of Christians — and of the title "Lord", which in the biblical tradition designates divine sovereignty itself, attributed to the risen Jesus.

These four titles prepare the way for the presentation, in the following articles, of the great mysteries of the life of Christ: incarnation, passion, death, resurrection, ascension and coming in glory.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part One, Section Two, Chapter Two, Article 2, nos. 422-451
Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed

itens.titulo: Creed: the Incarnation and the Mysteries of the Life of Christ
itens.resumo: The Catechism's commentary on the virginal conception, the birth of Christ, and the mysteries of his hidden and public life, up to the eve of the Passion.
itens.corpo:
This passage comments on the article of the Creed "conceived by the power of the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary." It explains why the Word became flesh, sets out the dogma of the hypostatic union — true God and true man in one Person — and treats the virginal conception of Jesus and the divine motherhood of Mary, "ever-Virgin."

The Catechism then goes through the "mysteries of the life of Christ": the hidden life at Nazareth, the baptism in the Jordan, the temptations in the desert, the proclamation of the Kingdom, the miracles, the Transfiguration, and the messianic entrance into Jerusalem, showing how the whole earthly life of Jesus is revelation and a work of salvation, not only its final moments.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part One, Section II, Chapter II, Article 3, nos. 456-570

itens.titulo: Creed: the Passion, Death and Burial of Christ
itens.resumo: The Catechism's commentary on the article "suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died and was buried".
itens.corpo:
This article deals with the trial and condemnation of Jesus, situating it within Christ's relationship with Israel and rejecting any reading that attributes to the Jewish people, as such, collective responsibility for his death. It sets out the saving meaning of Christ's death on the cross, willed by the Father "not as blind violence", but as part of the divine plan of redemption, in which Christ offered himself freely out of love.

The Catechism also treats the burial of Christ, showing it as the extreme point of his self-emptying (kenosis) and, at the same time, the sabbath rest that announces the resurrection — "Christ remained in the tomb between Friday afternoon and Easter Sunday".
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part One, Section Two, Chapter Two, Article 4, nos. 571-630
Council of Chalcedon (451), Definition of the Faith

itens.titulo: The Creed: The Resurrection and Ascension of Christ
itens.resumo: The Catechism's commentary on the descent into hell, the resurrection on the third day, and Christ's ascension into Heaven.
itens.corpo:
This passage comments on the articles "he descended into hell; on the third day he rose again from the dead" and "he ascended into heaven, and is seated at the right hand of God the Father almighty." It explains that the "descent into hell" means that Christ, truly dead, experienced the common condition of the dead and proclaimed the good news to the righteous who had gone before him.

It then sets out the resurrection as a real and transcendent event, attested by the empty tomb and by the appearances, and as the proper work of the Most Holy Trinity, the foundation of all Christian faith. Finally, it treats the ascension: the definitive entry of Christ's humanity into the glory of God, which is not absence but a new form of presence that prepares for the coming of the Holy Spirit and the mission of the Church.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part One, Section Two, Chapter Two, Articles 5-6, nos. 631-667

itens.titulo: Creed: "I Believe in the Holy Spirit"
itens.resumo: The Catechism's commentary on the third Person of the Trinity: his joint mission with the Son and his action in the Church and in the sacraments.
itens.corpo:
Opening the chapter devoted to the Holy Spirit, the Catechism explains that only faith makes it possible to fully recognize the Spirit in his joint and indivisible action with the Father and the Son, and it surveys the names, symbols, and revelations of the Holy Spirit throughout the Old and New Testaments — in the theophanies, in the prophets, at the Annunciation, at the baptism of Jesus, and above all at Pentecost.

The text insists that the mission of Christ and the mission of the Holy Spirit are "joint and inseparable": it is through the Spirit that the Church knows Christ, celebrates the sacraments, and is led into "all the truth," and it is the same Spirit who acts in each believer through gifts and charisms.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part One, Section Two, Chapter Three, Article 8, nos. 683-747
Second Vatican Council, Dogmatic Constitution "Lumen Gentium" (1964), no. 4

itens.titulo: Creed: The Church and the Communion of Saints
itens.resumo: The Catechism's commentary on the article "I believe in the Holy Catholic Church": the mystery, the four marks, the members, and the communion of saints.
itens.corpo:
This is the longest article in the commentary on the Creed. It treats the Church as mystery — the image of the "People of God," the "Body of Christ," and the "Temple of the Holy Spirit" —, sets out the four marks that characterize her (one, holy, catholic, and apostolic), and distinguishes the diversity of members within her: hierarchy, lay faithful, and consecrated life, each with its own vocation within the one mission of the Church.

The chapter then treats the communion of saints — the spiritual solidarity among the faithful on earth, those who already enjoy the vision of God, and those who are still being purified — and closes with the commentary on the figure of Mary, "Mother of Christ" and, for this reason, "Mother of the Church and Mother of men," the last subsection of the article devoted to the Church in the Creed.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part One, Section II, Chapter III, Article 9, nos. 748-975
Second Vatican Council, Dogmatic Constitution "Lumen Gentium" (1964)

itens.titulo: Creed: "the forgiveness of sins"
itens.resumo: The Catechism's commentary on the article of the Creed about the forgiveness of sins: Baptism and the power of the keys entrusted to the Church.
itens.corpo:
This brief article explains that the Christian faith inseparably links the profession of faith in God, Christ and the Church to the forgiveness of sins: "there is no other means of obtaining the forgiveness of sins" than in Christ and through the Church. It first deals with Baptism as the sacrament instituted for the forgiveness of sins, one and unrepeatable.

It then sets out the "power of the keys", entrusted by Christ to the Apostles and exercised in a proper way in the sacrament of Penance, by which sins committed after Baptism can be forgiven. It is the doctrinal foundation, within the Creed, on which the second part of the Catechism will later develop the sacrament of Reconciliation in greater detail.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part One, Section Two, Chapter Three, Article 10, nos. 976-987

itens.titulo: Creed: the Resurrection of the Body and Life Everlasting
itens.resumo: The last two articles of the Creed: faith in the final resurrection of the body and the last things — particular judgment, Heaven, Purgatory, Hell, and the Last Judgment.
itens.corpo:
Commenting on the final two articles of the Creed, the Catechism first explains what it means to believe in "the resurrection of the body": not merely the immortality of the soul, but the resurrection of each person's own body, in the likeness of the risen Christ, and how one should live from now on in view of this hope, "dying with Christ Jesus."

It then treats "life everlasting," going through what the Church believes about the moment of each person's death: the immediate particular judgment, the beatitude of Heaven as the vision of God face to face, the purification of Purgatory for those who die in grace but still imperfectly purified, the real possibility of Hell as the consequence of a definitive choice against God, and the Last Judgment that will crown history, when the risen bodies will be reunited with their souls forever.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part One, Section Two, Chapter Three, Articles 11-12, nos. 988-1065
1 Corinthians 15:20-26

itens.titulo: Part Two: The Celebration of the Christian Mystery
itens.resumo: The sacramental economy and the seven sacraments: how the salvation celebrated in the liturgy is communicated, together with the other liturgical celebrations (sacramentals and funerals).
itens.corpo:
The second part of the Catechism of the Catholic Church, entitled "The Celebration of the Christian Mystery" and corresponding to paragraphs 1066-1690, presents the faith as "celebrated": it sets forth the liturgy as the work of the Most Holy Trinity and the action of Christ and of the Church. According to the apostolic constitution "Fidei Depositum," with which John Paul II promulgated the Catechism on October 11, 1992, this part exists because "the Christian mystery is celebrated and communicated in the liturgical acts." There the sacramental economy is explained: the sacraments are efficacious signs of grace, instituted by Christ and entrusted to the Church, by which "the fruit of our Redemption is accomplished."

The part is organized in two sections. The first, "The Sacramental Economy" (nos. 1076-1209), comprises two chapters: the first, "The Paschal Mystery in the Age of the Church" (nos. 1077-1134), treats the liturgy as the work of the Trinity, the action of Christ, and the presence of the Holy Spirit and of the Church; the second, "The Sacramental Celebration of the Paschal Mystery" (nos. 1135-1209), answers who celebrates, how, when, and where it is celebrated, and treats liturgical diversity and the unity of the mystery. The second section, "The Seven Sacraments of the Church" (nos. 1210-1690), arranges the sacraments in three groups: those of Christian initiation — Baptism (no. 1213), Confirmation (no. 1285), and the Eucharist — those of healing — Penance and the Anointing of the Sick — and those at the service of communion — Holy Orders (no. 1536) and Matrimony (no. 1601).

The part closes with a chapter on "the other liturgical celebrations" (nos. 1667-1690), devoted to sacramentals (no. 1667) and Christian funerals (no. 1680), which include "the Christian's last Passover" and the celebration of the funeral rites. Thus, the second part answers the question "how we celebrate and receive what we believe."

The systematic treatment of the liturgy in this part is indebted to the renewal of the Council. The constitution "Sacrosanctum Concilium" on the Sacred Liturgy, approved on December 4, 1963, at the close of the second session of the Second Vatican Council, presided over by Pope Paul VI, with 2,147 votes in favor and only 4 against, was the first document promulgated by the Council — and the first time in the history of the Church that an ecumenical council devoted an entire document of its own to the liturgy. The structure of the Catechism also takes up the "ancient order" already followed by the Catechism of Saint Pius V: the Creed, the liturgy with the sacraments, the commandments, and prayer. The drafting of the work, then coordinated by Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, the future Benedict XVI, was decided upon after the Extraordinary Synod of Bishops of 1985 and took six years of work.

Second Vatican Council, Constitution "Sacrosanctum Concilium" on the Sacred Liturgy, December 4, 1963 (nos. 1-2)

itens.titulo: Part Two: The Sacramental Economy
itens.resumo: The liturgy as the work of the Most Holy Trinity and the common structure of the liturgical celebration, before the presentation of each sacrament in particular.
itens.corpo:
This section opens the second part of the Catechism by explaining why the liturgy is, above all, the work of God: the Father is the source and goal of the liturgy, Christ continues in it the work of his Paschal Mystery through the Church, "his Body and his Bride," and the Holy Spirit prepares the faithful for the encounter with Christ, makes present and actualizes the mystery of Christ, and unites the Church to the life and mission of Christ.

The text then deals with the liturgical celebration itself — who celebrates, how it is celebrated, when and where it is celebrated — presenting the elements common to every liturgical action (signs and symbols, word and music, sacred images) before the Catechism moves on, in the following section, to each of the seven sacraments.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part Two, Section One, nos. 1076-1209
Second Vatican Council, Constitution "Sacrosanctum Concilium" (1963)

itens.titulo: The Sacraments of Christian Initiation (Overview)
itens.resumo: The Catechism's overall view of Baptism, Confirmation, and the Eucharist as a single process of initiation into the Christian life.
itens.corpo:
Before treating each sacrament individually, the Catechism presents the three sacraments of Christian initiation — Baptism, Confirmation, and the Eucharist — as a unity: "by the sacraments of Christian initiation, man receives the foundations of the Christian life." It is through them that the faithful are born anew to a new life, are strengthened by the grace of the Holy Spirit, and are nourished by the Eucharistic food.

This chapter serves as an introduction to the three articles that follow, each devoted to one of these sacraments, and explains why the Church considers it essential that their unity — today often lived in a chronologically separated way, especially between Confirmation and the Eucharist — be preserved theologically and pastorally.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part Two, Section II, Chapter I, nos. 1212-1419
Catechism of the Catholic Church, Compendium, no. 250

itens.titulo: Baptism (Sacrament of Christian Initiation)
itens.resumo: The Catechism on Baptism: its signs and rites, its effects on the soul, who may receive and confer it, and its necessity for salvation.
itens.corpo:
This article treats Baptism as "the gateway to life in the Spirit" and "the door which gives access to the other sacraments," and as the foundation of the whole Christian life. It surveys the signs and rites of the baptismal celebration (water, anointing, white garment, candle), its institution by Christ, and its prefiguration throughout the Old Testament.

It then sets out the effects of Baptism: the forgiveness of original sin and of all personal sins, birth into a new life as a child of God, incorporation into Christ and the Church, and the indelible mark (the "character") that makes Baptism unrepeatable. It also deals with who can and should be baptized, including the Baptism of infants, and with the necessity of Baptism for salvation, without excluding hope for those who die without Baptism for reasons beyond their control.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part Two, Section II, Chapter I, Article 1, nos. 1213-1284
Second Vatican Council, Constitution "Sacrosanctum Concilium" (1963), no. 6

itens.titulo: Confirmation (Sacrament of Christian Initiation)
itens.resumo: The Catechism on Confirmation: its place in Christian initiation, the rite of anointing with chrism, and its effects of strengthening baptismal grace.
itens.corpo:
This article presents Confirmation as the sacrament that "perfects baptismal grace," uniting the faithful more firmly to Christ and enriching them with a special gift of the Holy Spirit, so that they may bear witness to the faith as true witnesses of Christ. It goes through the signs of the celebration, above all the anointing with holy chrism, and the sacramental formula proper to each rite (Latin and Eastern).

The text explains the effects of Confirmation — the outpouring of the Holy Spirit as at Pentecost, the increase and deepening of baptismal grace, an indelible spiritual character — and deals with who can and should receive it, the ordinary minister (the Bishop), and the conditions required of the person to be confirmed.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part Two, Section II, Chapter I, Article 2, nos. 1285-1321
Acts 2:1-4

itens.titulo: The Eucharist (Sacrament of Christian Initiation)
itens.resumo: The Catechism on the Eucharist as the source and summit of the Christian life: its institution by Christ, the real presence, and the sacramental sacrifice.
itens.corpo:
This is one of the longest articles of the Catechism. It treats the Eucharist as the "source and summit of the whole Christian life," sets out the names by which the Church designates it (the Breaking of Bread, the Holy Sacrifice of the Mass, Holy Communion, among others), and reviews the figures of the Old Testament and the institution by Jesus at the Last Supper, "on the night he was betrayed."

The text presents the liturgical celebration of the Mass, the mystery of the Eucharistic sacrifice — which makes present, without repeating it, the one sacrifice of the Cross — and the doctrine of the real presence of Christ under the species of bread and wine, through transubstantiation. Finally, it deals with the fruits of Communion and the conditions for receiving it worthily.

itens.titulo: Penance and Reconciliation (a sacrament of healing)
itens.resumo: The Catechism on the sacrament of confession: the conversion of the baptized who sin, the acts of the penitent, and sacramental absolution.
itens.corpo:
This article deals with the sacrament by which "those who approach obtain pardon from God's mercy for the offense committed against him." It explains why the baptized need a path of conversion and penance throughout life, and it traces the history of this sacrament in the Church, from the rigor of the ancient penance to the current practice of individual and frequent confession.

The Catechism sets out the acts of the penitent — contrition, confession, and satisfaction — and the role of the priest, who acts "in the person of Christ," as well as the spiritual effects of the sacrament: reconciliation with God and with the Church, remission of the eternal punishment, and, at least in part, of the temporal punishments due to sin. It also treats the sacramental seal and specific forms such as general absolution.

itens.titulo: The Anointing of the Sick (Sacrament of Healing)
itens.resumo: The Catechism on the sacrament intended for the gravely ill and the elderly: its biblical foundations, the rite, and its spiritual effects.
itens.corpo:
This article sets out the biblical foundation of the Anointing of the Sick, above all in the Letter of James ("Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the presbyters of the Church..."), and explains that this sacrament is not intended only for the moment of death — correcting the old use of the term "Extreme Unction" — but for every member of the faithful who begins to be in danger of death because of illness or old age.

The text deals with the celebration, centered on the anointing with oil and the priest's prayer of faith, and with its effects: a special gift of the Holy Spirit that comforts and strengthens the soul of the sick person, unites him to the Passion of Christ, can bring the forgiveness of sins when the sick person has not been able to confess, and at times even contributes to the recovery of health, "if it is beneficial to the salvation of his soul."
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part Two, Section II, Chapter II, Article 5, nos. 1499-1532

itens.titulo: Holy Orders (a Sacrament at the Service of Communion)
itens.resumo: The Catechism on the sacrament of Holy Orders: its three degrees — episcopate, presbyterate, and diaconate — and the meaning of the ordained ministry.
itens.corpo:
This article deals with the sacrament through which the mission entrusted by Christ to the Apostles continues to be exercised in the Church until the end of time. It explains the three degrees of the sacrament of Holy Orders — the episcopate, which confers the fullness of the ministerial priesthood, the presbyterate, co-worker of the Bishops, and the diaconate, ordained for service — and the central rite of each ordination: the laying on of hands followed by the consecratory prayer.

The text sets forth the proper effect of this sacrament, an indelible spiritual character that configures the ordained man to Christ the Head, Shepherd, and Servant of the Church, and addresses who may receive it — reserved to baptized men — and the canonical conditions for ordination, including the discipline of celibacy in the Latin Church.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part Two, Section II, Chapter III, Article 6, nos. 1536-1600
Second Vatican Council, Decree «Presbyterorum Ordinis» (1965)

itens.titulo: Matrimony (a Sacrament at the Service of Communion)
itens.resumo: The Catechism on the sacrament of Matrimony: its origin in creation, its elevation by Christ, its essential properties, and its goods.
itens.corpo:
This article treats marriage as a reality already inscribed in the work of creation — "It is not good that the man should be alone" — and raised by Christ to the dignity of a sacrament, a sign of the covenant between Christ and the Church, his Bride. It covers the celebration of marriage, the free consent of the spouses as the element that "makes" the marriage, and the proper role of the spouses as ministers of this sacrament to each other.

The Catechism sets out the essential properties of marriage — unity and indissolubility — and its goods, above all openness to fertility and the education of children. It also addresses pastorally delicate situations, such as mixed marriages, disparity of cult, and the difficulties faced by divorced faithful, while reaffirming the doctrine on the indissolubility of the bond.

itens.titulo: Sacramentals and Christian Funerals
itens.resumo: The final chapter of the second part: the sacramentals instituted by the Church and the liturgical meaning of the Christian funeral.
itens.corpo:
Closing the second part, this chapter first deals with the sacramentals — sacred signs instituted by the Church, distinct from the seven sacraments, which prepare the faithful to receive the fruit of the sacraments and sanctify various circumstances of life: blessings, consecrations of persons and objects, exorcisms, among others. It also explains popular piety as a legitimate, though imperfect, expression of faith.

The second part of the chapter deals with Christian funerals, explaining why the Church accompanies with her liturgical prayer the passage of the faithful to the Father: the funeral liturgy celebrates the paschal mystery of Christ, expresses communion with the deceased, and proclaims the hope of eternal life, being distinguished from the farewell rites of different cultures by its Christological center.

itens.titulo: Part Three: Life in Christ
itens.resumo: The dignity of the person, the human community, grace, and the Ten Commandments, which the Catechism comments on following the division of Saint Augustine.
itens.corpo:
The third part of the Catechism (nos. 1691-2557) deals with the Christian moral life on the basis of man's vocation to beatitude. It opens by citing Saint Leo the Great: "Christian, recognize your dignity" (no. 1691), and is organized into an Introduction (nos. 1691-1698) and two Sections. The First Section, "Man's Vocation: Life in the Spirit" (no. 1699), unfolds in three chapters: "The Dignity of the Human Person" (nos. 1700-1876), which starts from man created in the image of God and goes through beatitude, freedom, the morality of human acts, the passions, moral conscience, the virtues, and sin; "The Human Community" (nos. 1877-1948), on the person and society, the common good, authority, social justice, and solidarity; and "God's Salvation: Law and Grace" (nos. 1949-2051), which distinguishes the natural moral law, the Old Law, and the New Law or Law of the Gospel, and deals with justification, grace, merit, and holiness, concluding with the Church as "mother and teacher" (nos. 2030ff).

The Second Section, "The Ten Commandments" (nos. 2052-2557), begins with the episode of the rich young man ("Teacher, what good deed must I do to have eternal life?", Mt 19:16) and shows that Jesus did not abolish the Law but brought it to perfection, associating the evangelical counsels with the commandments (no. 2053). There follows a chapter on the first three commandments, concerning the love of God (nos. 2083-2195), and another on the remaining seven, concerning the love of neighbor (nos. 2196-2557). The Catechism explicitly records that the division and numbering of the commandments have varied over history and that "the present Catechism follows the division of the commandments established by Saint Augustine" (no. 2066), the same as that of the Lutheran confessions, whereas the Greek Fathers adopted a different division, maintained in the Orthodox Churches and the Reformed communities.

This part engages intensively with the Second Vatican Council. The Pastoral Constitution Gaudium et Spes — "The Church in the Modern World," promulgated by Paul VI on December 7, 1965, approved by 2,307 bishops against 75, and the longest conciliar document — is a constant source for the doctrine on human dignity, community, the common good, and social justice. Vatican II is also cited in texts such as no. 1705, on freedom as "an exceptional sign of the divine image," and no. 1776, on human conscience.

itens.titulo: Part Three: The Dignity of the Human Person and the Vocation to Beatitude
itens.resumo: The opening of Catholic morality in the Catechism: man created in the image of God and called, through the Beatitudes, to the happiness that only God can give.
itens.corpo:
This entry corresponds to Chapter One of Part Three of the Catechism. The boundaries should be made precise: Part Three as a whole is titled "Life in Christ" (nos. 1691-2557) and opens with Section One, "Man's Vocation: Life in the Spirit" (no. 1699). Within it, Chapter One is "The Dignity of the Human Person" (nos. 1700-1876), whose first two articles — "Man: The Image of God" (no. 1700) and "Our Vocation to Beatitude" (no. 1716) — are the subject of this exposition; it is on this anthropological foundation that all the morality that follows rests.

Part Three takes up again what the faith confessed in Part One. No. 1691 opens it with a quotation from Saint Leo the Great: "Christian, recognize your dignity and, now that you share in God's own nature, do not return to your former base condition by a life unworthy of that dignity." No. 1692 explains the passage: what the Creed professes, the sacraments communicate; through the sacraments Christians have become "children of God" (1 Jn 3:1) and "partakers of the divine nature" (2 Pet 1:4), and for this reason they are called to lead a life worthy of the Gospel. Christian morality is thus presented as a consequence of the dignity received, not as an external code.

No. 1700 summarizes the program of the Chapter: "The dignity of the human person is rooted in his creation in the image and likeness of God (Article 1); it is fulfilled in his vocation to divine beatitude (Article 2)." In Article 1, the Catechism states that it was in Christ, "the image of the invisible God" (Col 1:15), that man was created in the image of the Creator, and that it was also in Christ the Redeemer that this image, "disfigured in man by the first sin, has been restored to its original beauty and ennobled by the grace of God." The human person is defined as "the only creature on earth that God has willed for its own sake," endowed with "a spiritual and immortal soul" (no. 1703), destined from conception for eternal beatitude. Through reason he is able to understand the order of things established by the Creator; through his will, to direct himself toward his true good — and in this freedom, "an eminent sign of the divine image," his dignity is found and, at the same time, his responsibility in the face of sin, which has wounded human nature (no. 1714).

Article 2 (no. 1716) deals with the vocation to beatitude. The Beatitudes, the text says, "are at the heart of Jesus' preaching"; they take up the promises made to the chosen people since Abraham and fulfill them, but by ordering them no longer to the possession of a land, but to the Kingdom of heaven. No. 1717 states that they "depict the countenance of Jesus Christ and portray his charity," express the vocation of the faithful "associated with the glory of his Passion and Resurrection," and are "paradoxical promises that sustain hope in the midst of tribulations," already inaugurated in the life of the Virgin Mary and of all the saints.

Then comes the desire for happiness. No. 1718 states that the Beatitudes "respond to the natural desire for happiness," a desire of divine origin that God placed in the human heart "in order to draw man to the One who alone can fulfill it." Here the Catechism relies explicitly on Saint Augustine, citing the *Confessions*: "How is it then that I seek you, Lord? Since in seeking you, my God, I seek a happy life, let me seek you so that my soul may live," concluding with the summary "God alone satisfies." No. 1723 then sets out the doctrine of false happinesses: true happiness "is found neither in riches or well-being, nor in human fame or power, nor in any human achievement... nor in any creature, but in God alone." The text also draws on a quotation about modern idols, in which "riches are the great divinity of this age" and fame has become "a good in itself, a sovereign good, an object of genuine veneration."

Nos. 1724-1727 close the article by showing the concrete paths to the Kingdom — "the Decalogue, the Sermon on the Mount, and the apostolic catechesis" — and summarizing the ultimate end to which God calls man: "the Kingdom, the vision of God, participation in the divine nature, eternal life, filial adoption, rest in God." The beatitude of eternal life is presented as a gratuitous and supernatural gift, not as a human achievement.

itens.titulo: Part Three: Man's Freedom
itens.resumo: The Catechism on human freedom as the root of moral responsibility, its conditioning factors, and its relationship with grace.
itens.corpo:
This article defines freedom as "the power, rooted in reason and will, to act or not to act, to do this or that," which makes the human being the subject of morally imputable acts. It explains that freedom attains its perfection when it is directed toward God, the supreme Good, and that the more one does what is good, the freer one becomes.

The Catechism also deals with the factors that can diminish or nullify the imputability of an act — ignorance, habit, violence, fear, and other psychological or social factors — and explains the relationship between human freedom and salvation: each person is responsible for the acts they perform deliberately, without this denying the necessity of God's grace for acting well.

itens.titulo: Part Three: The Morality of Human Acts and of the Passions
itens.resumo: What makes a human act morally good or evil, according to the Catechism, and the role of the passions — such as joy, fear or anger — in the moral life.
itens.corpo:
This passage sets out the three elements that determine the morality of a human act: the object chosen, the intention (the end), and the circumstances. It explains that a good act requires all three to be good at the same time, and that certain acts are always illicit "by reason of their object" "in themselves and by themselves", regardless of circumstances or intention — the so-called intrinsically evil acts.

Next, the Catechism treats the passions — the emotions and movements of the sensitive appetite such as love, hatred, desire, joy, sadness, fear and anger —, teaching that they are in themselves neither good nor evil, but receive moral quality according to whether they are in fact ordered by reason and will to good or to evil.

itens.titulo: Part Three: The Moral Conscience
itens.resumo: The Catechism on the moral conscience as the "most secret core" of the person, its formation, and the difference between a upright conscience and an erroneous conscience.
itens.corpo:
This article defines the moral conscience as the practical judgment of reason that tells each person, at the moment of acting, whether a particular concrete act is good or evil, exercising, with regard to that act, "the function of witness, guide, and judge." It insists that every person must follow the certainty of his conscience, even when it may be mistaken.

The Catechism then deals with the formation of conscience — a lifelong task, supported by the Word of God, the teaching of the Church, and the counsel of people of upright conscience — and distinguishes the upright and true conscience from moral error, explaining the different causes of ignorance or error of conscience and the way each of them affects the responsibility of the agent.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part Three, Section I, Chapter I, Article 6, nos. 1776-1802
Second Vatican Council, Pastoral Constitution "Gaudium et Spes" (1965), no. 16

itens.titulo: Part Three: The Virtues
itens.resumo: The Catechism on virtue as a habitual disposition to do good: the four cardinal virtues and the three theological virtues.
itens.corpo:
This article defines virtue as "a habitual and firm disposition to do the good," which enables the person not only to perform good acts, but to give the best of himself. It sets out the four cardinal virtues — prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance — which structure human moral life and around which all the other moral virtues are organized.

The text then treats the three theological virtues — faith, hope, and charity — which have God as their origin, motive, and immediate object, are infused by God into the souls of the faithful, and ground and animate the exercise of all the moral virtues. It closes with a note on the gifts and fruits of the Holy Spirit, which perfect the virtues of those who receive them.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part Three, Section I, Chapter I, Article 7, nos. 1803-1845

itens.titulo: Part Three: Sin
itens.resumo: The Catechism on the nature of sin, the distinction between mortal and venial sin, and the reality of the proliferation of sin.
itens.corpo:
Closing the first chapter of the third part, this article defines sin as "an offense against reason, truth, and right conscience", an offense against God and neighbor through a disordered love for some good, and explains the diversity of sins according to their object, the virtues or commandments to which they are opposed, and whether they concern God, neighbor, or oneself.

The Catechism sets forth the fundamental distinction between mortal sin — which destroys charity in the heart of man by a grave violation of God's law, in grave matter, with full knowledge and deliberate consent — and venial sin, which weakens charity without breaking it. Finally, it treats the proliferation of sin, including the notion of structures of sin that result from the accumulation of personal sins.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part Three, Section I, Chapter I, Article 8, nos. 1846-1876

itens.titulo: The Ten Commandments: The First Commandment
itens.resumo: The Catechism's commentary on the commandment "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart": faith, hope, charity, and the sins against religion.
itens.corpo:
Opening the commentary on the Ten Commandments, this article treats the first of them in the light of the twofold commandment of love taught by Christ. It sets out the theological virtues as man's response to God's love — faith, hope, and charity — and the virtue of religion, which disposes man to render to God the worship and adoration that are due to him.

The Catechism then goes on, at length, to examine the sins that are opposed to this first commandment: against faith (incredulity, heresy, apostasy, voluntary doubt), against hope (despair, presumption), against charity (indifference, ingratitude, lukewarmness, hatred of God), and against the virtue of religion — superstition, idolatry, divination, magic, irreligion, atheism, and agnosticism. It also deals with the prohibition of images and of swearing false oaths.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part Three, Section Two, Chapter One, Article 1, nos. 2084-2141

itens.titulo: The Ten Commandments: The Second Commandment
itens.resumo: The Catechism's commentary on the commandment concerning the name of God (nos. 2142-2167): respect for the holy name, the upright oath and the vow, and the prohibition of blasphemy, perjury and the magical use of the divine name.
itens.corpo:
The second commandment — "You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain" (Ex 20:7; Dt 5:11) — belongs, like the first, to the sphere of the virtue of religion and regulates in a particular way our use of speech in sacred matters (no. 2142). The Catechism opens its commentary by recalling that, among all the words of Revelation, there is one that is unique: the name of God himself, which he entrusts to those who believe in him and reveals in his personal mystery. The gift of the name belongs to the order of trust and intimacy; therefore man must not abuse it, but must keep it in memory "in loving adoring silence" and use it only to bless, praise and glorify (no. 2143).

The text recalls that, in the Old Covenant, the divine name was surrounded by awe: revealed to Moses as the unpronounceable tetragrammaton, it was replaced in reading by the Hebrew word Adonai ("my Lord") and, in the Greek version of the Septuagint, translated as Kyrios ("Lord"). This same title passes into the New Testament applied to Jesus, whose name means that God himself is present in the person of his Son made man: "there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved" (Acts 4:12). The faithful must therefore bear witness to the name of the Lord, confessing their faith without yielding to fear, and preaching and catechesis must be permeated with adoration and respect for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ (no. 2145).

The Catechism then distinguishes upright uses from abuses. Every improper use of the name of God, of Jesus Christ, of the Virgin Mary and of the saints is forbidden (no. 2146). Promises made to others in God's name engage the divine honor, fidelity, truthfulness and authority, and must, in justice, be honored: to be unfaithful to them is to misuse God's name and, in some way, to make God out to be a liar (no. 2147). The oath — calling on God as witness to the truth (Dt 6:13) — is lawful when taken in truth, in judgment and in justice, following the example of Saint Paul, but the holiness of the divine name demands that one not have recourse to it for trivial matters (nos. 2150, 2154-2155). The vow, a deliberate and free promise made to God, likewise binds by virtue of divine fidelity.

The final part deals with sins against this commandment. Blasphemy — using in an injurious way the name of God, of Christ, of the Virgin and of the saints, or speaking ill of God interiorly or exteriorly — "is directly opposed to the second commandment" and is, in itself, a grave sin (nos. 2148, 2162). It extends to words against the Church and sacred things and, in a particular way, to the use of God's name to cover up crimes, to reduce peoples to servitude, to torture or to put to death. A false oath calls on God to witness a lie, and perjury is a grave offense against the Lord, who is always faithful to his promises (no. 2163). Also condemned are "oaths" that invoke the name of God without intending blasphemy, and the magical use of the divine name (no. 2149).

Finally, the Catechism links the commandment with the Christian name: Baptism is conferred "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Mt 28:19), and the Christian receives his name in the Church, preferably that of a saint, who offers him a model of charity and a guarantee of intercession (no. 2156). Each man's name is sacred, because it is the icon of the person (no. 2158), and the sign of the cross, "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit," consecrates the day to the glory of God (no. 2157). The summary of the Catechism sums everything up in the acclamation of Psalm 8: "O Lord, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth!" (no. 2160).

itens.titulo: The Ten Commandments: The Third Commandment
itens.resumo: The Catechism's commentary on the commandment of Sabbath rest: the Lord's Day, Sunday rest, and the precept of Sunday Mass.
itens.corpo:
This article deals with the third commandment, the precept of Sabbath rest inherited from the Old Testament and transformed, through the resurrection of Christ, into the "Lord's Day," Sunday. It explains the meaning of the Israelite Sabbath as a memorial of creation and of the liberation of the Exodus, and how the Church, from apostolic times, began to celebrate the weekly Passover on the first day of the week.

The Catechism treats the obligation to participate in the Sunday Eucharist, one of the fundamental precepts of Christian life, and the meaning of Sunday as a day of rest from servile work, devoted to joy, family life, and works of mercy, without thereby excluding work that is truly necessary for society.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part Three, Section II, Chapter One, Article 3, nos. 2168-2195

itens.titulo: The Ten Commandments: The Fourth Commandment
itens.resumo: The Catechism's commentary on the commandment to honor father and mother: duties within the family and the extension of this commandment to relations with civil authority.
itens.corpo:
This is the first of the commandments that deal with love of neighbor, and it opens the second tablet of the Law. The Catechism discusses the reciprocal duties between parents and children: the respect, gratitude, obedience, and assistance that children owe their parents, and the duty of parents to bring up their children in the faith, respecting them as persons and as children of God.

The text then extends the meaning of the commandment beyond the nuclear family, treating the duties of the members of the wider family and, above all, of civil authority: citizens owe obedience and cooperation to legitimate authorities, which in turn must exercise power in service of the common good, respecting the fundamental rights of the person. It also deals with the duties of society toward the family.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part Three, Section II, Chapter Two, Article 4, nos. 2197-2257

itens.titulo: The Ten Commandments: The Fifth Commandment
itens.resumo: The Catechism's commentary on the commandment "You shall not kill": respect for human life, abortion, euthanasia, legitimate defense, and peace.
itens.corpo:
This is one of the longest articles in the commentary on the commandments, dealing with the respect owed to human life from conception until natural death, "because it is sacred, for from its beginning it involves the creative action of God." It surveys the prohibition of direct and voluntary homicide, procured abortion, and euthanasia, condemned as gravely contrary to the moral law, and it also deals with suicide, showing why the Church continues to pray for those who take their own lives.

The Catechism then turns to respect for the dignity of persons — care of health, the prohibition of experiments, mutilations, and kidnapping —, to respect for the soul of the neighbor in regard to scandal, to legitimate defense and the death penalty, and finally to peace and war, setting out the classic conditions of the "just war" and condemning the disproportionate arms race.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part Three, Section II, Chapter Two, Article 5, nos. 2258-2330

itens.titulo: The Ten Commandments: The Sixth Commandment
itens.resumo: The Catechism's commentary on the commandment "You shall not commit adultery": the vocation to chastity, conjugal love, and the fruitfulness of marriage.
itens.corpo:
This article deals with human sexuality and the universal vocation to chastity, the virtue that integrates sexuality into the person in a unified way. It explains the different forms of chastity — of the unmarried, of the married, of those who live celibacy or consecrated virginity — and the offenses against this virtue: masturbation, fornication, pornography, prostitution, and homosexual acts, while teaching the respect and welcome owed to every person, regardless of his or her inclination.

The text then deals with the love of spouses in marriage, the goods and demands of conjugal love — fidelity and fruitfulness — and responsible parenthood, including the Church's teaching on the regulation of births and the rejection of artificial contraceptive means. It concludes by treating the offenses against the dignity of marriage: adultery, divorce, polygamy, and free union.

itens.titulo: The Ten Commandments: The Seventh Commandment
itens.resumo: The Catechism's commentary on the commandment "You shall not steal": respect for the goods of others, private property, social doctrine, and care for creation.
itens.corpo:
This article deals with the respect owed to the goods of others and with the right use of material goods. It sets forth the universal destination of goods and private property as a legitimate right, yet subordinated to the common good, and it condemns theft, the unjust retention of the goods of others, commercial fraud, corruption, and every deliberate damage to private or public property.

The text extends the commandment to the principles of the Church's social doctrine — justice and solidarity among nations, economic activity and social justice, human work as participation in the work of the Creator — and to respect for the integrity of creation, dealing with the responsible use of natural resources and of animals. Finally, it deals with the preferential option for the poor.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part Three, Section Two, Chapter Two, Article 7, nos. 2401-2463

itens.titulo: The Ten Commandments: The Eighth Commandment
itens.resumo: The Catechism's commentary on the commandment "You shall not bear false witness": truth, lying, secrecy, and the right use of the media.
itens.corpo:
This article deals with the duty to live in the truth and to bear witness to it, even in the face of difficulties. It sets out the sins against the truth — false witness and perjury, rash judgment, detraction and calumny, flattery and lying — and the obligation to make reparation for offenses committed against the honor and reputation of others.

The Catechism then treats respect for the truth and the duty of discretion, including professional secrecy and the sacramental seal, which require prudence in communication, and concludes with a reflection on the use of the social communications media, which must be at the service of truth, freedom, justice, and solidarity.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part Three, Section II, Chapter Two, Article 8, nos. 2464-2513

itens.titulo: The Ten Commandments: The Ninth Commandment
itens.resumo: The Catechism's commentary on the commandment against coveting the flesh: the purification of the heart and the struggle against concupiscence.
itens.corpo:
This article comments on the commandment "You shall not covet your neighbor's wife," which the catechetical tradition distinguishes from the tenth commandment because it deals specifically with disordered desire connected with sexuality. It explains that Baptism confers on the one baptized the grace of purifying the heart, but that the concupiscence of the flesh remains as an inclination to be fought throughout life, with the help of grace.

The Catechism treats the purification of the heart as a condition for "seeing God," according to the sixth Beatitude, and the battle for purity, which requires the virtue of chastity, modesty, and the purification of the gaze and of the imagination itself, placing this struggle within the broader context of the spiritual battle against disordered inclinations.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part Three, Section II, Chapter II, Article 9, nos. 2514-2533

itens.titulo: The Ten Commandments: The Tenth Commandment
itens.resumo: The Catechism's commentary on the commandment against coveting the goods of others: detachment, spiritual desire, and poverty of heart.
itens.corpo:
Concluding the exposition of the Ten Commandments, this article deals with the commandment that forbids coveting the goods of one's neighbor, going beyond mere outward respect for the property of others (already treated in the seventh commandment) to also require interior detachment from material goods. It explains the difference between natural and legitimate desire, for example that of obtaining what is necessary for oneself and for others, and disordered covetousness, the root of thefts, robberies, and frauds.

The Catechism then deals with spiritual desire, teaching that the human heart is made to desire God above all things, and comments on the poverty of heart proclaimed in the first Beatitude as the way to be freed from covetousness and to place all hope in the heavenly Father, "who lacks nothing."
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part Three, Section II, Chapter Two, Article 10, nos. 2534-2557

itens.titulo: Part Four: Christian Prayer
itens.resumo: Prayer as gift, covenant and communion, its three expressions, and the battle of prayer; and the commentary on the Our Father, "the summary of the whole Gospel."
itens.corpo:
The fourth and final part of the Catechism (nos. 2558-2865) presents prayer as the "living and personal relationship with the living and true God" that springs from the faith professed, celebrated, and lived in the three preceding parts. It opens with a classic definition, taken from Saint John Damascene: "Prayer is the raising of one's mind and heart to God or the requesting of good things from God" (no. 2559), completed by the description of Saint Thérèse of Lisieux: "For me, prayer is a surge of the heart; it is a simple look turned toward heaven, it is a cry of recognition and of love, embracing both trial and joy." The text insists that prayer is above all a gift of God rather than a human work: "man is a beggar before God" (no. 2559), and that humility is its foundation, for "we do not know how to pray as we ought" (Rom 8:26).

The First Section, "Prayer in the Christian Life" (nos. 2558-2758), is organized in three chapters. The first traces the Revelation of prayer: in the Old Testament, in the figures of Abraham, Jacob, Moses, David, and the prophets (nos. 2568ff); in "the fullness of time," in the filial prayer of Christ and the prayer of the Virgin Mary and her "Fiat" (nos. 2598ff); and in the time of the Church, distinguishing the five fundamental forms — blessing and adoration, petition, intercession, thanksgiving, and praise (nos. 2623ff). The second chapter, "The Tradition of Prayer" (nos. 2650-2696), deals with the "sources" (the Word of God, the Liturgy, the theological virtues) and the "way" of prayer, with its spiritual guides. The third, "The Life of Prayer" (nos. 2697-2758), sets out the three expressions preserved by Tradition — vocal prayer, meditation, and contemplative prayer, which "have one basic trait in common: composure of heart" (no. 2699) — and describes the battle of prayer with its difficulties: distraction, dryness, acedia, and the "humble vigilance of heart," concluding with filial confidence.

The Second Section, "The Lord's Prayer: 'Our Father'" (nos. 2759-2865), is a systematic commentary on the prayer taught by Jesus. The Catechism recalls that Tertullian called it breviarium totius Evangelii — "the summary of the whole Gospel" (no. 2761) — and that the Didache, at the end of the first century, already prescribed praying it three times a day. The commentary goes through the prologue ("Our Father who art in heaven"), in which the "daring to approach the Father with complete trust" is underscored, and then the seven petitions, one by one, closing with the final doxology ("For the kingdom, the power, and the glory are yours, now and forever"), whose absence in some manuscript traditions the Catechism notes.

The structural criterion of the whole part is made explicit in no. 2857: the first three petitions have as their object the glory of the Father (the sanctification of the Name, the coming of the Kingdom, the fulfillment of his will), and the last four present our needs to him (bread, forgiveness, victory over temptation and over the Evil One). It is the part that answers the question of how we speak to God about what we believe, celebrate, and live.

itens.titulo: Part Four: The Revelation of Prayer
itens.resumo: The Catechism traces the biblical history of prayer, from the Old Testament to the prayer of Jesus and the prayer of the nascent Church.
itens.corpo:
This chapter opens the fourth part of the Catechism by surveying the "surprising fact" of prayer throughout all of Scripture. It deals with prayer in the Old Testament — creation as the first call to prayer, the prayer of Abraham, Jacob, Moses, the Psalms as the prayer school par excellence — and shows how Israel's prayer matures throughout the history of salvation.

The text then turns to the prayer of Jesus, setting out how He prayed and how He taught us to pray, and concludes with prayer in the age of the Church: the prayer of Mary and the Apostles, prayer in the community of Jerusalem, and the different forms of prayer that the Christian Tradition recognizes from these biblical sources.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part Four, Section I, Chapter I, nos. 2566-2649

itens.titulo: Part Four: The Tradition of Prayer
itens.resumo: The Catechism on the living sources of Christian prayer, its expressions — vocal prayer, meditation, and contemplation — and the great teachers and places of prayer.
itens.corpo:
This chapter deals with the sources of the life of prayer handed down by Tradition: the Word of God, the liturgy of the Church, the theological virtues, and the concrete situations of daily life. It also presents "the cloud of witnesses" — figures of saints throughout history — and the different paths of prayer proper to the various spiritualities.

The text goes through the three great expressions of the life of prayer: vocal prayer, which involves the body and the voice; meditation, which seeks God through reflection, through books, above all Scripture; and contemplative prayer, "a gaze of faith fixed on God," which Saint Teresa of Jesus described as "a close sharing between friends." It also addresses places favorable to prayer, such as the church, the monastery, and the Christian home.

itens.titulo: Part Four: The Life of Prayer
itens.resumo: The Catechism on prayer throughout the Christian life, its privileged moments, its difficulties, and the spiritual battle it requires.
itens.corpo:
This chapter treats prayer as something that should permeate every moment of the Christian life — the Liturgy of the Hours, the Eucharist, the Rosary, devotion to the Virgin Mary — and the communal and personal expressions that complement one another. It also deals with the different times of the day and of life that are especially favorable to prayer.

The last section of this chapter, "the battle of prayer," is one of the most candid in the Catechism about the concrete difficulty of praying: the common objections against prayer, distraction, dryness, lack of faith and of perseverance. The text teaches humility, filial trust and perseverance as fundamental attitudes in the face of these difficulties, and comments on the prayer of Jesus' hour in Gethsemane as a model of the spiritual battle of prayer.

itens.titulo: The Our Father: "the summary of the whole Gospel"
itens.resumo: The opening of the Catechism's commentary on the Our Father (nos. 2761-2776): the patristic tradition that calls it the "summary of the whole Gospel," its centrality in Scripture, and its place in the liturgy of the Church.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism begins its commentary on the Lord's Prayer under the title "The summary of the whole Gospel." The phrase is taken from Tertullian, who in *De Oratione* (1,6) writes that "the Lord's Prayer is truly the summary of the whole Gospel"; in the same passage, the African author adds that, after bequeathing us this formula, the Lord commanded us to "ask and you will receive" (Jn 16:24), so that each one may direct other prayers to heaven according to his needs, "but always beginning with the Lord's Prayer, which remains the fundamental prayer" (no. 2761).

The text situates the Our Father "at the center of the Sacred Scriptures" (no. 2762). Taking up the reflection of Saint Augustine — who, after showing how the Psalms converge on the petitions of the Lord's Prayer, concludes that there is no prayer in the Scriptures that is not contained in it — the Catechism shows that the prayer taught by Jesus gathers and sums up all Christian prayer. Saint Thomas Aquinas, in the *Summa theologiae* (II-II, q. 83, a. 9), calls it "the most perfect of prayers"; and the Catechism observes that the version handed down by Matthew (6:9-13), longer than that of Luke (11:2-4), was the one adopted from the earliest centuries in the liturgy and in catechesis.

Several ancient sources attest to the use of the prayer from the early Church. The *Didache*, or "Teaching of the Twelve Apostles" (1st-2nd century), in chapter 8, commands that it be prayed "three times a day," making explicit its catechetical function before Baptism; the *Apostolic Constitutions* (7,24,1) and the homilies of Saint John Chrysostom confirm its constant presence in the life of the community. The Catechism observes that most of the patristic commentaries on the Our Father were addressed to catechumens and neophytes, because it is the people of the "newborn" in Baptism who pray and obtain mercy (no. 2769).

It is called the "Lord's Prayer" because it comes to us from the Lord Jesus, teacher and model of our prayer (no. 2775). The Catechism underlines its liturgical centrality: it is the prayer of the Church par excellence, an integral part of the major "hours" of the Divine Office and of the sacraments of Christian initiation — Baptism, Confirmation, and the Eucharist (no. 2776). Inserted into the Eucharistic liturgy, between the anaphora and the communion rite, it recapitulates all the petitions of the celebration and, at the same time, "knocks at the door of the feast of the Kingdom" which Communion anticipates (no. 2770). In this position it also manifests the eschatological character of its petitions: it is the prayer proper to the "end time," begun with the outpouring of the Spirit and destined to end with the return of the Lord (no. 2771). The Roman liturgical tradition, as devotional sources recount, attributes to Saint Gregory the Great (pope from 590 to 604) the placing of the Our Father immediately before the breaking of the bread, a position the Mass preserves to this day — although this fact is transmitted as tradition, without unambiguous contemporary documentation.

The Church thus prays "until he comes" (1 Cor 11:26): the Eucharist and the Our Father strain together toward the coming of the Lord, and the seven petitions express the groanings of the present time, during which "it does not yet appear what we shall be" (1 Jn 3:2).

itens.titulo: The Our Father: "Our Father who art in heaven"
itens.resumo: The Catechism's commentary on the opening invocation of the Our Father (nos. 2777-2802): the filial boldness of calling God Father, the meaning of "our" and of the phrase "who art in heaven."
itens.corpo:
Before commenting on the seven petitions, the Catechism pauses over the invocation that opens the Lord's Prayer, under the heading "Our Father who art in heaven" (nos. 2777-2802). The text begins with the confidence with which the Church addresses God: in the Roman liturgy, the Eucharistic assembly is invited to pray to the Father "with the confidence of children," and the Eastern liturgies use similar expressions: "dare to call upon," "make us worthy." Before the burning bush, Moses was told: "Do not come near; put off your shoes from your feet" (Ex 3:5); only Jesus could cross this threshold of the divine holiness, and it is he who, having made purification for sins (Heb 1:3), brings us into the presence of the Father (no. 2777).

The Catechism gives this filial impulse the Greek name that the liturgies of the East and the West have consecrated: *parrhesía*, that is, "straightforward simplicity, filial trust, joyous assurance, humble boldness, the certainty of being loved" (no. 2778). Saint Peter Chrysologus, in Sermon 71, expresses this paradox: "The awareness we have of our condition as slaves would make us sink into the ground, our earthly condition would dissolve into dust, if the authority of our Father himself and the Spirit of his Son did not impel us to cry out: 'Abba, Father!'" (Rom 8:15). Before making this first word its own, the Catechism asks that the heart be purified of false paternal or maternal images, for God "transcends the created order," and to transfer our ideas to him would be to "fashion idols to adore or pull down" (no. 2779).

Turning to the word "Father," the text explains that we can invoke God in this way because he was revealed to us by his Son made man and because the Spirit makes him known to us. The personal relationship of the Son to the Father, which man cannot conceive and which the angels cannot glimpse, is shared by the Spirit of the Son with those who believe in Jesus (no. 2780). The translation "Father" corresponds to the Aramaic term *abbâ*, which expresses the intimacy and trust of a filial relationship lived by Jesus and communicated to the disciples.

The first word of the prayer is, before it is a petition, a blessing of adoration: "the glory of God is that we recognize him as Father, the true God" (no. 2781). The pronoun "our" excludes every individualistic appropriation of prayer: in saying "Our Father," we invoke the New Covenant in Christ, communion with the Most Holy Trinity, and the divine charity which, through the Church, extends to the dimensions of the world (no. 2801). Calling God Father presupposes the adoptive filiation received in Baptism, by which we are incorporated into Christ and made children in the only Son (no. 2798). The Lord's Prayer puts us in communion with the Father and with the Son and, at the same time, reveals us to ourselves (no. 2799).

As for the phrase "who art in heaven," the Catechism emphasizes that it "does not refer to a place but to God's majesty and his presence in the hearts of the just." Heaven, the Father's house, is the true homeland toward which we are journeying and to which we already belong (no. 2802): Christians "are in the flesh, but they do not live according to the flesh; they spend their lives on earth, but they are citizens of heaven." The Lord's Prayer thus appears integrated into the Eucharist, manifesting the eschatological character of its petitions, in the hope of the Lord, "until he comes!" (1 Cor 11:26).

itens.titulo: The Our Father: First Petition — "Hallowed Be Thy Name"
itens.resumo: The Catechism's commentary on the first petition of the Our Father: the request that God's name be recognized as holy in us and in the whole world, and the connection of this sanctification to Baptism.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism comments on the first of the seven petitions of the Our Father in paragraphs 2807-2815, in Part Four, Section II, Article 3. Above all, it observes that, although God's name is holy in itself, "The verb 'to hallow' is to be understood here not primarily in its causative sense (only God hallows, makes holy) but above all in an evaluative sense: to recognize as holy, to treat in a holy way." This invocation is therefore also understood, in adoration, as praise and thanksgiving. In praying it, the believer enters into God's plan to hallow his name — revealed to Moses and then in Jesus — "by us and in us, as well as in every nation and in each man" (no. 2858; cf. Ez 36:23).

The text rests on the patristic tradition. It cites Saint Cyprian of Carthage (c. 200-258), bishop and martyr, in his treatise on the Lord's Prayer: "How could God, whom no one can sanctify, since he is himself the source of all holiness, be sanctified by us? But because he himself said: 'Be holy, for I am holy,' we ask and pray that, having been sanctified in Baptism, we may persevere in what we have begun to be. And this we ask every day. We need daily sanctification so that, falling into faults every day, we may be cleansed from them by an assiduous sanctification. Therefore, we pray that this sanctification may remain in us." The Catechism also stresses that we do not say "hallowed be thy name in us," but simply "thy name," because we ask that it be hallowed in all men — as Saint Augustine prayed, for whom the petition includes those who are still to believe.

The petition is inseparably bound to the life and prayer of the believer: on it depends whether God's name is hallowed among the nations. It is the first of the three petitions "more theological," which have as their object the glory of the Father (nos. 2803-2806). The Catechism recalls that the prayer we offer to the Father is ours if it is prayed "in the name" of Jesus, and cites Christ's priestly prayer: "Holy Father, keep them in thy name, which thou hast given me" (Jn 17:11). Baptism, which incorporated us into Christ and made us holy, is the foundation of this sanctification in which we are to persevere; the Catechism connects the petition to the desire that baptismal consecration give life to our whole existence (cf. 1 Thes 4:7).

The broader context of Part Four explains that Saint Luke preserved a short text of the Our Father (five petitions) and Saint Matthew a more developed version (seven petitions), and that the liturgical tradition of the Church has retained Matthew's text (Mt 6:9-13; no. 2759). Saint Thomas Aquinas, cited by the Catechism (no. 2763), teaches that the Lord's Prayer "is the most perfect of prayers," since in it "we ask not only for everything we can rightly desire, but also in the sequence that we should desire them."

itens.titulo: The Our Father: the Second Petition — "Thy Kingdom Come"
itens.resumo: The Catechism's commentary on the second petition of the Our Father: the request for the definitive coming of the Kingdom of God, already present but not yet fulfilled, and the Church's "Maranatha."
itens.corpo:
The Catechism comments on the second petition of the Our Father in paragraphs 2816-2821, in Part Four, Section II, Article 3. It begins by noting that, in the New Testament, the same Greek word "basileia" can be translated as kingship (abstract noun), kingdom (concrete noun), or reign (noun of action), which already indicates the richness and ambiguity of the expression "Kingdom of God." The Kingdom is before us: it drew near in the incarnate Word, was proclaimed throughout the whole Gospel, and came in the death and Resurrection of Christ; it has been coming since the Last Supper and, in the Eucharist, it is in our midst. It will come, however, in glory, when Christ hands it over to his Father. The Catechism here welcomes the interpretation that the Kingdom itself can mean Christ in person, "whom we desire every day to come, and whose coming we wish to be manifested to us quickly," for, as he is our resurrection, so "he can also be the Kingdom of God, for in him we shall reign."

This petition is identified with the "Maranatha," the cry of the Spirit and the Bride: "Come, Lord Jesus!" (1 Cor 16:22; Rev 22:20). The Catechism observes that, even without the obligation imposed by this prayer, we would spontaneously have uttered this cry, eager to embrace the object of our hope. Here lies the central eschatological tension: the Kingdom is already present in grace and in the Eucharist, but has not yet reached its fullness — the "already" and the "not yet" of the theology of the Kingdom.

The text also stresses the moral dimension and discernment. It cites Rom 14:17 — "The Kingdom of God is righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit" — and observes that only a pure heart can say with confidence "Thy Kingdom come"; one must have learned from Paul to say: "Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal bodies" (Rom 6:12). Christians must, by discernment in the Spirit, distinguish between the growth of the Kingdom of God and the progress of culture and society, without separating the one from the other: man's vocation to eternal life does not suppress, but rather reinforces, the duty to put into practice the energies and means received from the Creator in the service of justice and peace in this world (no. 2820).

The Catechism recalls that this petition is made and heard in the prayer of Jesus, present and effective in the Eucharist, and that, among the seven petitions, this one — like the others — is sustained by the prayer of Christ. The Compendium of the Catechism (no. 590) sums up: the Church asks for the final coming of the Kingdom through Christ's return in glory, but also prays that the Kingdom may grow "even now," thanks to the sanctification of men in the Spirit and the commitment to justice and peace. At bottom, the commentary takes up a controversy of modern theology about the nature of the Kingdom — between the readings that emphasize its future dimension and those that emphasize its present one — and resolves it in the doctrine that the Kingdom came with Christ, remains in the mystery of the Church, and will be consummated in glory.
