itens.titulo: The Our Father: The Third Petition — "Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven"
itens.resumo: The Catechism's commentary on the third petition: to ask that God's saving will be accomplished in us and in the world, in the image of Christ's obedience in Gethsemane.
itens.corpo:
In nos. 2822-2827, the Catechism comments on the third petition of the Our Father. It begins by affirming that the Father's will is saving and universal: it is God's will "that all men should be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth" (1 Tim 2:3-4), for He "is patient [...], not wishing that any should perish" (2 Pet 3:9). And it adds that the commandment which "sums up all the others and tells us His whole will" is "that you love one another as I have loved you" (no. 2822).

The text then distinguishes two levels of the divine will. There is God's will "made known to us in the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure which he set forth in Christ [...]: to unite all things in him" (Eph 1:9-11) — the eternal plan to sum up all things in Christ, which we ask to be "fully accomplished on earth as it is already in heaven" (no. 2823). And there is the historical fulfillment of this plan in Christ's human will: "It was in Christ and through his human will that the Father's will was perfectly fulfilled once and for all" (no. 2824), for upon coming into the world He said: "Behold, I have come to do your will, O God" (Heb 10:7).

The central point of the third petition is the prayer in the agony in Gethsemane. Jesus, who could say "I always do what is pleasing to him" (Jn 8:29), at the hour of the Passion conforms himself entirely to the Father's will: "Not my will, but yours, be done" (Lk 22:42). The Catechism sees in this "yes" the model of the petition: we ask that our will be united to Christ's so that the plan of salvation may be fulfilled. It acknowledges, however, our powerlessness: "We are radically incapable of this, but united to Jesus and with the power of his Holy Spirit, we can surrender our will to him and decide to choose what his Son has always chosen" (no. 2825). "By adhering to Christ, we can become one spirit with him, and thereby fulfill his will; in this way it will be perfectly accomplished on earth as in heaven."

The last part refers to discernment and to the ecclesial and universal dimension of the petition. It is through prayer that "we can discern what is the will of God and obtain the endurance to do it" (no. 2826), for one does not enter the Kingdom "by words, but by doing the will of my Father who is in heaven" (Mt 7:21). And the Catechism emphasizes that the petition is made in communion with the Church, "with the all-holy Mother of God and with all the saints," and that its scope is cosmic, not individualistic — as the patristic quotation gathered in no. 2827 says: Jesus "does not say 'Thy will be done' in me or in you, but 'in all the earth': so that error may be banished from it and truth reign in it, vice be destroyed and virtue flourish, and so that the earth may no longer differ from heaven." In this vein, the Commentary on the Catechism breaks with any reading of mere passive resignation: it is a matter of active and loving discernment, uniting the prayer of the faithful still on earth to the already full "yes" of the saints in Heaven.

itens.titulo: The Our Father: the Fourth Petition — "Give us this day our daily bread"
itens.resumo: The Catechism's commentary on the fourth petition of the Our Father: the request for material sustenance and, above all, for the Eucharistic Bread of Life.
itens.corpo:
Opening the series of the four petitions that "commend our weakness to the grace of the Father", the Catechism explains this petition in its most immediate sense: the trusting request for the food necessary for survival each day, an expression of filial abandonment to Providence and, at the same time, a call to solidarity with those who go hungry.

The text also sets out the deeper meaning of this petition in the tradition of the Church, which reads it as a reference to the Bread of Life — the Word of God and, above all, the Body of Christ received in the Eucharist — and comments on the adverb "this day", linked to the manna in the desert and to God's "today", which teaches us to trust in the present without anxiety about the future.

itens.titulo: The Our Father: the Fifth Petition — "Forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive those who trespass against us"
itens.resumo: The Catechism's commentary (nos. 2838-2845) on the fifth petition of the Our Father, which links the forgiveness received from God to the readiness to forgive those who have offended us, without limit or measure.
itens.corpo:
In its commentary on the fifth petition of the Our Father (nos. 2838-2845), the Catechism begins by calling this petition "astonishing" (no. 2838). If it contained only its first part — "Forgive us our trespasses" — it could already be included in the first three petitions, since Christ's sacrifice is "for the forgiveness of sins." But the second part, "as we forgive those who trespass against us," introduces a requirement: our petition will not be heard unless we have first met this condition. The expression "as," the text observes, links a response that must precede the prayer.

No. 2839 describes the petition as a new beginning: although clothed in the baptismal garment, the faithful continue to sin and to turn away from God. In this petition they return to Him "like the prodigal son" and acknowledge themselves to be sinners "like the tax collector." The prayer begins with a confession in which "we acknowledge our wretchedness and His mercy"; firm hope rests on Christ, "in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins" (Col 1:14), and on the sacraments of the Church, "the effective and undoubted sign of His forgiveness." The Catechism also recalls that forgiveness is "a power that raises to new life and gives the courage to look to the future with hope."

The second part of the petition is commented on from no. 2842. Jesus' "as" is not an injunction to imitate God "from the outside," but an invitation to a vital participation, "coming from the depths of the heart," in the holiness, the mercy and the love of God. It is the Holy Spirit — "who is our life" (Gal 5:25) — who can make "our own" "the mind of Christ Jesus." The unity of forgiveness then becomes possible, "forgiving one another as God in Christ forgave us" (cf. Eph 4:32). Hence no. 2843: prayer cannot reach the Father without the readiness to forgive; refusal hardens the heart and closes it to the Father's merciful love. It is the Spirit who "turns the wound into compassion and purifies the memory, transforming the offense into intercession."

The two final paragraphs raise the theme to its summit. No. 2844 affirms: "Forgiveness is the high point of Christian prayer"; it extends even to the forgiveness of enemies, "transfigures the disciple, configuring him to his Master," and bears witness that "in our world love is stronger than sin" — a witness which, the Catechism notes, the martyrs give "of yesterday and today." It is also the "fundamental condition" of the reconciliation of the children of God with their Father and of people with one another. No. 2845 concludes that "there is no limit or measure to this essentially divine forgiveness," recalling that we are always debtors: "Owe no one anything, except to love one another" (Rom 13:8).

The reference to "seventy times seven" in Mt 18:21-22 — Jesus' answer to Peter, who had asked how many times he should forgive — confirms that the measure of Christian forgiveness is not human calculation, but God's own mercy. The Catechism thus relies on primary texts of the New Testament: the Our Father of Matthew (6:12, which says "debts") and of Luke (11:4, which says "sins"), the parable of the unforgiving servant (Mt 18:23-35) and the Pauline exhortation to mutual forgiveness.

itens.titulo: The Our Father: Sixth Petition — "And Lead Us Not into Temptation"
itens.resumo: The Catechism's commentary on the sixth petition of the Our Father (nos. 2846-2849), which clarifies that God tempts no one to evil, distinguishes trial from temptation, and asks for the Spirit of discernment, vigilance of heart, and final perseverance.
itens.corpo:
The sixth petition of the Our Father, commented on in nos. 2846-2849 of the Catechism, "goes to the root" of the preceding petition, since sins are the fruit of consenting to temptation. The Catechism observes that it is difficult to render the Greek verb of the original — "me eisenénkes" — with a single word: it means "do not allow us to enter into" and "do not let us yield to temptation." The central theological point is the distinction between being tempted and being the cause of temptation: "God cannot be tempted by evil and he himself tempts no one" (Jas 1:13). What is asked of the Father is not that he deliver us from every trial, but that he "not let us take the way that leads to sin," in the struggle between "the flesh and the Spirit."

No. 2847 unfolds this request into three discernments. The Holy Spirit makes us discern, first, "between trials, which make the inner man grow, and temptation, which leads to sin and death" — linked to the "tested virtue" of which Lk 8:13-15, Acts 14:22, 2 Tim 3:12 and Rom 5:3-5 speak (cf. Jas 1:14-15). Second, between "being tempted" and "consenting" to temptation. Third, discernment "unmasks the lie of temptation": its object appears "good, pleasing to the eyes, and desirable" (Gen 3:6), when in reality its fruit is death. Here the Catechism cites a passage from Origen, from the treatise De oratione (29, 15 and 17): "God never wants to impose good, but wants free beings. … There is a certain usefulness to temptation. No one but God knows what our soul has received from him, not even we ourselves. But temptation reveals it in order to teach us to know ourselves, and in this way we discover our wretchedness and are obliged to give thanks for the goods that temptation has revealed to us."

No. 2848 shows that "not entering into temptation" implies "a decision of the heart": "Where your treasure is, there will your heart be also. … No one can serve two masters" (Mt 6:21, 24). It is in this "consent" to the Holy Spirit that the Father gives us strength, according to the promise of Saint Paul: "God is faithful, and he will not let you be tested beyond your strength, but with the testing he will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it" (1 Cor 10:13). No. 2849 concludes that "such a battle and such a victory" are possible only through prayer: "it is by his prayer that Jesus vanquished the tempter, both at the outset of his public mission" — in the temptations in the desert (Mt 4:1-11; Mk 1:12-13) — "and in the final combat of his agony," in Gethsemane. It is to this battle of Christ that the faithful are united in this petition. The Catechism then associates the petition with "vigilance of the heart," which is the "guarding of the heart": Jesus asks the Father to "keep us in his name," and the Holy Spirit seeks to awaken us to it.

The petition "takes on its full dramatic meaning" when related to "the final temptation of our earthly struggle": it asks for final perseverance, under the warning of Revelation, "Behold, I am coming like a thief! Blessed is he who is awake" (Rev 16:15). The Compendium of the Catechism (§ 596) sums it up: in asking "lead us not into temptation," the faithful ask God the Father "not to leave us alone and at the mercy of temptation," and implore the Spirit "for the grace of vigilance and final perseverance."

The translation of this petition became the subject of public debate during the pontificate of Francis. In a 2017 interview on the program Padre Nostro (TV2000), the Pope stated that "a God who induces us into temptation is not a good translation," and explained: "It is I who fall into temptation; it is not God who throws me into it." The Italian Episcopal Conference approved a new version in November 2018, "non abbandonarci alla tentazione" ("do not abandon us to temptation"), confirmed by the Holy See and in use in the Italian Roman Missal since the first Sunday of Advent 2019. The Brazilian formula "não nos deixeis cair em tentação" ("do not let us fall into temptation") already expressed closeness to this sense, and the French version had, years earlier, changed from "ne nous soumets pas à la tentation" ("do not subject us to temptation") to "ne nous laisse pas entrer en tentation" ("do not let us enter into temptation"). The image accompanying the entry is the fresco Temptations of Christ, by Sandro Botticelli (1480-1482), in the Sistine Chapel, in which the three temptations in the desert appear in the upper register of the composition.

itens.titulo: The Our Father: The Seventh Petition — "But Deliver Us from Evil"
itens.resumo: The Catechism's commentary on the last petition of the Our Father, which embraces all the preceding ones in the request for deliverance from evil and from the Evil One.
itens.corpo:
The last of the seven petitions, this article explains that "evil" from which deliverance is asked does not designate an abstraction, but a person: Satan, the Evil One, the angel who opposes God. In this petition the Church asks that the victory already won by Christ over "the ruler of this world" be made manifest, and for deliverance from every evil, present, past, and future, of which he is the author or instigator.

The text explains why this last petition sums up and recapitulates all the preceding ones, entrusting to the Father all of their supplications, and comments on the final doxology, "For the kingdom, the power, and the glory are yours, now and for ever," and the "Amen" that seals all Christian prayer, concluding the Catechism's commentary on the Our Father and the entire fourth part.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part Four, Section Two, Article 3, nos. 2850-2854

itens.titulo: The Dogma of the Most Holy Trinity
itens.resumo: How the Church, on the basis of Revelation and not of reason alone, professes one God in three distinct and truly equal Persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
itens.corpo:
After setting forth faith in the one God, revealed to Israel, the Catechism turns to the "central mystery of Christian faith and life": only God can make himself known to us as Trinity, and this is what he did by sending his Son and the Holy Spirit. The Church received this revelation already in the baptismal formula — "in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit" (Mt 28:19) — and not "in the names," since there is but one God, not three.

In order to formulate this dogma without betraying either the divine unity or the real distinction of the Persons, the Church had to develop, over the course of the first councils, a terminology of its own — "substance," "person" or "hypostasis," "relation" — borrowed from philosophy, but with its own theological meaning. Thus the classic formula was reached: one single divine substance, nature, or essence in three Persons really distinct from one another, distinguished only by their relations of origin — the Father begets the Son, the Son is begotten, the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

The Catechism concludes this article by recalling that the ultimate end of the whole divine economy is to bring creatures into the perfect communion of the Blessed Trinity — which is why the Church, from Baptism onward, inserts every Christian into this very Trinitarian life.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part One, Section II, Chapter One, Article 1, Paragraph 2, nos. 232-267
Matthew 28:19

itens.titulo: God's Creation of the World
itens.resumo: The Catechism on creation as the free and good work of the Trinity, made out of nothing, and on divine providence in the face of the mystery of evil.
itens.corpo:
After treating the mystery of the Trinity, the Catechism turns to the work of creation: the world is not a necessary emanation of God, nor does it exist by chance, but proceeds freely from the divine goodness, "out of nothing" (ex nihilo) and not from preexisting matter. To create is, for God, to give existence to something entirely distinct from himself, yet which reflects him and is called to share in his goodness: "God saw that it was very good" (Gen 1:31).

The text insists that creation is the common work of the three Persons of the Trinity — "the operation of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit in creation is one and the same" — and explains that God does not abandon the created world to its own fate: he exercises over it a loving and constant providence, leading creation and human history to the end he has established, even though the concrete ways of this providence often escape human understanding.

It is at this point that the Catechism directly confronts the problem of evil and suffering in the face of an almighty and good Creator God, referring its full answer to the Paschal mystery of Christ: only in the light of faith can one accept, without a complete philosophical answer, that God knew how to bring a greater good even out of the greatest of moral evils, the abandonment of his own Son on the cross.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part One, Section Two, Chapter One, Article 1, Paragraph 4, nos. 279-314
Genesis 1

itens.titulo: Man, the Image of God
itens.resumo: The Catechism on the creation of the human being in the image and likeness of God, the unity of body and soul, sexual difference, and the state of original justice.
itens.corpo:
Distinct from the rest of the visible creation, man, according to the biblical account, is the only creature God willed "for its own sake," called to share, by knowledge and love, in God's own life. It is "in the image of God" that man and woman are created (Gen 1:27): capable of knowing and loving their Creator, set by him as masters of all visible creation to cultivate and care for it.

The Catechism insists on the unity of the human person, body and soul: the spiritual soul is not a part "added" to the body, nor is the body mere matter animated by some vital force. It is the deep unity of body and soul that constitutes, in Catholic doctrine, human nature itself, created directly by God. It also deals with the equal dignity of man and woman, created for one another in complementarity, and with the human vocation to interpersonal communion, already reflecting here something of the Trinitarian communion.

The chapter closes by describing the state of "original justice" in which Revelation places the first couple before sin: an interior harmony, with God, between the spouses, and with all of creation, soon broken by the disobedience recounted in the third chapter of Genesis.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part One, Section II, Chapter One, Article 1, Paragraph 6, nos. 355-384

itens.titulo: The Fall: Original Sin
itens.resumo: The Catechism on the biblical account of the first disobedience and the dogma of original sin transmitted to all humanity.
itens.corpo:
This chapter reads the account of Genesis 3 as a narrative that uses figurative language to affirm a real primordial event, which took place at the beginning of human history: the disobedience of Adam and Eve, seduced by the tempter into distrusting God's goodness, broke the original harmony between man and God, man with himself, between man and woman, and between humanity and all creation.

From this account, the Catechism sets forth the dogma of original sin: a state, not a personal act of each individual, transmitted to all humanity "by propagation, not by imitation", present in each person from conception as a deprivation of original holiness and justice, without this making human nature totally corrupted — it remains wounded in its natural powers, subject to ignorance, suffering, and the dominion of death, and inclined to sin, but essentially good.

The text underscores that this doctrine, somber at first sight, can only be fully understood in the light of Christ: it is "in the light of Christ the Redeemer" that original sin is revealed in all its gravity, and it is already in the very account of the fall that the hope of a future Redeemer is announced — the "protoevangelium" of Genesis 3:15, the oldest promise of salvation.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part One, Section II, Chapter One, Article 1, Paragraph 7, nos. 385-421
Genesis 3

itens.titulo: The Church: People of God, Body of Christ, Temple of the Holy Spirit
itens.resumo: The three biblical images with which the Catechism describes the nature of the Church before addressing her four marks.
itens.corpo:
Before commenting on the four marks of the Church (one, holy, catholic, and apostolic), the Catechism dwells on three complementary biblical images that express her deepest nature. As the "People of God," the Church gathers men and women from all nations, not by ties of blood, but by faith in Christ and by Baptism, called to live as a priestly, prophetic, and royal people in service of all humanity.

As the "Body of Christ," the Church is not merely a society of people united by common goals, but a vital communion with Christ, who constitutes her his Mystical Body through the Spirit and, in an eminent way, through the Eucharist: "we, though many, are one body, for we all partake of the one bread" (1 Cor 10:17). Christ is the Head of this Body, and the faithful, united to him, are also united among themselves as diverse and complementary members.

As the "Temple of the Holy Spirit," finally, the Church is the space in which the Spirit dwells, distributing to each member the gifts and charisms necessary for the building up of the whole Body, and is compared by the Catechism to the "soul" of the Mystical Body, the principle of its unity in the diversity of ministries, states of life, and charisms.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part One, Section II, Chapter Three, Article 9, Paragraph 2, nos. 781-810
1 Corinthians 10:17; 12:12-27

itens.titulo: The Marks of the Church: One, Holy, Catholic and Apostolic
itens.resumo: The Catechism's commentary on the four characteristics, inseparable from one another, that the Creed attributes to the true Church of Christ.
itens.corpo:
The Creed confesses the Church as "one, holy, catholic and apostolic" — four characteristics, or "notes," which theological tradition has always understood as inseparable from one another and as mutually illuminating. The Church is one because she has her origin and model in the unity of the Trinity, is founded by a single Lord, given life by a single Spirit, and gathers in a single faith, the same sacraments, and apostolic succession — which does not prevent, but rather requires, a legitimate diversity of gifts, rites, and traditions within this unity.

She is holy because Christ, her founder, is holy, and the Church is indissolubly united to him as his Bride; although her members, being sinners, always need purification and conversion, the Church already possesses the holiness of Christ in Mary and in the saints, and leads, through grace, to holiness of life.

She is catholic — "universal" — in the twofold sense of possessing within herself the fullness of the means of salvation entrusted by Christ and of being sent to all peoples, not limited by geographical or cultural boundaries. Finally, she is apostolic: founded on the Apostles, she guards and transmits their teaching and continues to be governed, under the assistance of the Holy Spirit, by their successors, the Bishops in communion with the successor of Peter.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part One, Section Two, Chapter Three, Article 9, Paragraph 3, nos. 811-870
Second Vatican Council, "Lumen Gentium" (1964), no. 8

itens.titulo: The Hierarchical Constitution of the Church
itens.resumo: The Catechism on the Christological origin of the ordained ministry and the hierarchical structure that serves, and does not dominate, the People of God.
itens.corpo:
This chapter deals with the way Christ organized his Church: he himself instituted various ministries, ordered to the good of the whole Body, entrusting a sacred power of service, not of domination — "whoever would be first among you must be slave of all" (Mk 10:44). This authority is exercised collegially by the College of Bishops, successors of the Apostles, always in communion with the Bishop of Rome, successor of Peter and visible head of this college.

The text explains the threefold office (munus) entrusted to the Bishops — teaching, sanctifying and governing — and how priests and deacons cooperate in this ministry in distinct and complementary degrees, all at the service of the same mission of the Church. It also deals with the proper role of the College of Bishops, exercised in a solemn manner in the ecumenical councils, and with the relationship between the Petrine primacy and episcopal collegiality, two principles that the Second Vatican Council sought to articulate without contradiction.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part One, Section II, Chapter III, Article 9, Paragraph 4, nos. 874-896
Second Vatican Council, "Lumen Gentium" (1964), nos. 18-29

itens.titulo: Mary, Mother of Christ and Mother of the Church
itens.resumo: The Catechism's commentary on Mary's role in the Church, proclaimed "Mother of the Church" by Paul VI at the close of Vatican II.
itens.corpo:
Concluding the article of the Creed devoted to the Church, the Catechism addresses Mary's unique place within it. Recognized since the first centuries as "Mother of God" (Theotókos, a title defined at the Council of Ephesus, 431), Mary is also, as a consequence, the true mother of the members of Christ, "for she cooperated by her charity in the birth of believers in the Church, who are members of its Head."

The text recalls that, at the close of the third session of the Second Vatican Council, on November 21, 1964, Pope Paul VI solemnly proclaimed Mary "Mother of the Church, that is to say, of all the Christian people, both the faithful and the pastors" — a title that expresses, in synthetic form, Mary's spiritual motherhood over the whole Church, and not only over Christ according to the flesh.

The Catechism also addresses the cult of veneration (hyperdulia) offered to Mary, distinct from the adoration due to God alone, and Marian piety as a legitimate and desirable expression of the Christian faith, which finds in Mary "the figure of the Church" — the first and most perfect disciple of Christ.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part One, Section II, Chapter III, Article 9, Paragraph 6, nos. 963-975
Paul VI, closing address of the 3rd session of the Second Vatican Council (November 21, 1964)

itens.titulo: The Natural Moral Law
itens.resumo: The Catechism on the natural moral law: the moral sense, inscribed by God in human reason, which makes it possible to discern good and evil before any revealed or civil law.
itens.corpo:
The Catechism defines the natural law as man's participation, through his reason, in the wisdom and goodness of the Creator: an original moral sense, "written and engraved in the soul of each and every man" (cf. Rom 2:14-16), which enables him, even without explicit revelation, to discern the good that he must do and the evil that he must avoid. This law sets forth the first and essential precepts that govern the moral life — starting from the first principle, "good is to be done and evil is to be avoided" — from which more particular precepts derive.

The text deals with the universality of this law — present, in varied formulations, in the great wisdom traditions of humanity — and with its immutability in its most general principles, even though its concrete application is, in history, permeated by weakness and sin, which can obscure a clear perception of its demands.

It is on this natural moral law, common to every human being, that the Catechism grounds the possibility of moral dialogue between believers and non-believers, and the legitimacy of civil law, which finds in it its necessary foundation: without the natural law, the Catechism warns, the very moral structure of societies loses a rational basis shared by all.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part Three, Section I, Chapter III, Article 1, nos. 1954-1960
Romans 2:14-16

itens.titulo: The Old Law and the New Law, or Law of the Gospel
itens.resumo: The Catechism on the Law revealed to Israel and its fulfillment in the New Law of Christ, which interiorizes the commandments through the grace of the Spirit.
itens.corpo:
After treating the natural law, the Catechism sets forth the "Old Law," that is, the Ten Commandments and the other precepts revealed by God to Israel through Moses. Although still imperfect — "a pedagogy" that prepares and disposes the people for conversion and faith, without of itself giving the interior strength to fulfill it — the Old Law already expresses many truths accessible to natural reason and remains valid in its moral precepts, which Christ took up and deepened.

The "New Law," or Law of the Gospel, is "the perfection here on earth of the divine law, natural and revealed" brought about by Christ, above all in the Sermon on the Mount: it does not abolish the Old Law, but fulfills, surpasses, and perfects it, raising its promises to the Beatitudes of the Kingdom of Heaven and transforming its commandments by reaching the root of acts, the heart.

The Catechism insists that the New Law is, first and foremost, "the grace of the Holy Spirit given to the faithful through faith in Christ" — a law of love, of grace, and of freedom, not merely a new external code, even though it is also expressed in concrete moral teachings, contained in the Gospels and in the apostolic letters.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part Three, Section I, Chapter III, Article 1, nos. 1961-1974
Matthew 5-7

itens.titulo: Grace and Justification
itens.resumo: The Catechism on grace as the free gift of God that justifies the sinner, and the distinction between grace and merit.
itens.corpo:
This article treats justification, the work of the grace of the Holy Spirit who cleanses us of our sins and communicates to us "the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ" (Rom 3:22), accomplished definitively by Baptism and continually renewed in the Christian life. Justification includes the remission of sins, sanctification, and the renewal of the interior man, uniting the believer, through faith and the sacraments, to the passion and resurrection of Christ.

The Catechism then defines grace as "the favor, the free and undeserved help that God gives us to respond to his call" — an absolutely gratuitous gift, which no human merit can precede or provoke, carefully distinguishing between actual grace (God's particular interventions) and habitual grace (the permanent state of life in God), and between grace and the various charisms and graces of state.

Finally, the text treats merit: the Christian, once justified by grace, can truly merit, for himself and for others, an increase of grace, of charity, and of eternal life — but even this merit is, in its ultimate root, the fruit of God's grace, not man's autonomous achievement, so that "our justification comes from the grace of God," never from a supposed acquired right before him.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part Three, Section I, Chapter III, Article 2, nos. 1987-2029
Romans 3:21-26

itens.titulo: The Church, Mother and Teacher: The Moral Magisterium
itens.resumo: The Catechism on the authority of the Church's pastors to teach and discern questions of morality in the light of the Gospel.
itens.corpo:
This article deals with the mission of the Church, "the pillar and bulwark of the truth" (1 Tim 3:15), to proclaim continually the moral principles, including those of the social order, and to make judgments about any human matter insofar as the fundamental rights of the human person or the salvation of souls require it. It explains that this task is ordinarily carried out by the pastors through catechesis and preaching, taking the Decalogue as the central reference, common to the moral conscience of every human being.

The Catechism also deals with the authority of the Roman Pontiff and of the Bishops in communion with him to teach the faith and morals authentically to the People of God, and with the scope of the infallibility of the Magisterium in moral matters: it extends to all the elements of doctrine, including moral doctrine, without which the saving truths of the faith cannot be preserved, expounded, or observed with fidelity.

Finally, the text emphasizes that this doctrinal authority does not replace, but serves the conscience of each believer, offering it the light needed to form it rightly in the face of concrete and often complex moral situations.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part Three, Section I, Chapter III, Article 3, nos. 2030-2051
1 Timothy 3:15

itens.titulo: The Ten Commandments in Sacred Scripture and in Tradition
itens.resumo: The Catechism's introduction to the second section of Part Three, on the biblical origin of the Decalogue and its permanent reading by the Tradition of the Church.
itens.corpo:
Before commenting on each of the Ten Commandments individually, the Catechism places the Decalogue within the history of salvation: given by God to Moses on Sinai as part of the Covenant with Israel, the Decalogue is not an arbitrary list of prohibitions, but the explication, in ten words, of the fundamental demands of love of God and love of neighbor — the first three commandments turned more directly toward the love of God, the following seven toward the love of neighbor.

The text insists that the Decalogue forms "an organic unity," in which each commandment refers to the whole: transgressing a single one already wounds the whole Law, although not all the commandments carry the same weight in the hierarchy of the values they express. It also explains that fidelity to Scripture and the example of Jesus himself — who, to the rich young man, points directly to the commandments (Mt 19:16-19) — led the Tradition of the Church to recognize in the Decalogue a primordial importance in Christian moral catechesis from the first centuries.

The chapter closes by explaining why, although its content is already largely accessible to reason through the natural law, the Christian receives the Decalogue in the light of grace: what God commands, he himself makes possible to fulfill through his grace, linking the moral demand of the Decalogue with the promise of the New Covenant.
fontes: Catechism of the Catholic Church, Part Three, Section II, Introduction, nos. 2052-2082
Matthew 19:16-19
